sections.h2: Selling a house fast in Union, NJ
sections.html:
The quickest sale in Union is a cash purchase by an investor or family buyer who takes the property in its present state and orders the township's resale inspection. A listing suits a well kept house in a sought-after pocket, and selling without an agent is permitted. Every route needs a resale certificate before closing, so the inspection decides your timeline more than the buyer does.

Union here means Union Township in Union County, not Union City in Hudson County. The township has 63,675 people on 9.05 square miles of land. About 71.5% of its 21,374 households own their home, and the median owner-occupied value is $451,300. Owners with a mortgage pay a median of $3,015 a month, and those without one pay $1,292. Homes range from older houses in Putnam Manor to newer pockets near Kean University and the train station.

People in Union describe where they live by neighborhood more than by township name, so use the name buyers know when you write a listing.

  • Five Points, around the junction of Galloping Hill Road, Chestnut Street and Salem Road.
  • Union Center, near Morris and Stuyvesant Avenues.
  • Vauxhall, north of Interstate 78, with its own ZIP code, 07088.
  • Putnam Manor and Putnam Ridge, an older residential section off Colonial Avenue and Morris Avenue.
  • Battle Hill, in the west near the Rahway River and Route 22, and Larchmont Estates by the Larchmont Reservation.
  • Green Lane, a newer community between Kean University and Union Station.

Union requires a Residential Resale Certificate, also called a certificate of continued occupancy, before a sale. Requests must be made at least ten business days before the inspection date, and the certificate is not issued until the inspection fee is paid. The visit verifies smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and fire extinguishers. Every open permit must be closed with the proper inspections first.

Inspections run on weekdays from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. The owner or a representative must be at the house during those hours, or a second visit is scheduled at an added charge. The certificate is issued two full business days after final approval and stays valid for three months unless occupancy or ownership changes. It cannot be transferred.

The checklist is short and concrete, so a seller can prepare in a weekend.

  • At least one smoke detector on each level, plus one within 10 feet of each separate sleeping area. Two-family houses also need one at the top of each common stairwell.
  • Carbon monoxide alarms outside each sleeping area, within 10 feet of the bedroom doors.
  • A fire extinguisher within 10 feet of the kitchen, no smaller than 2A:10B:C and no larger than 10 pounds, mounted no more than five feet off the floor and in plain view.
  • Smoke alarms mounted to the manufacturer's directions with no double-sided tape, and the extinguisher on a hanger or bracket.
  • Existing hardwired detection systems from a newer build or renovation kept working, since battery units are not accepted as replacements.

Test every alarm before the inspector arrives. A failed visit means another $80 and another wait. A cash buyer will often fix these small items before closing so the certificate can issue.

sections.h2: How long the resale process takes
sections.html:
Plan on at least two to three weeks from request to certificate. The township wants ten business days of notice before the inspection, and the certificate comes two full business days after final approval. If the first visit fails, the housing inspector books a second one, which adds the $80 fee and another wait.

Because the certificate lasts three months, you can apply as soon as a contract is signed without much risk of it lapsing before closing. When the buyer wants a quick closing, apply the day the contract is signed. Ask the township whether any permits on the house, such as a finished basement or a deck, are still open, since the inspection cannot pass until they are closed.

A short order of operations helps. Pull your permit history first. Close anything open. Replace old alarms and mount an extinguisher near the kitchen. Then submit the request and put the inspection date in the sales contract so the buyer knows what to expect.

On closing day, bring the certificate to the table. The title company and the buyer's attorney will want to see it, along with proof that open permits were closed and the Tax Office's latest payment status. A cash buyer usually skips the lender's extra conditions, so these papers are often all that remains between the signed contract and the deed.

Union property taxes are due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a 10-day grace period. Postmarks do not count as proof of payment, so a payment must be physically in the Tax Office by 4:30 p.m. to be credited that day. A drop box at the front door of the municipal building on Morris Avenue works around the clock, and cash should never go in it.

The Tax Office collects municipal, county and school taxes and sewer utility bills. Bills equal assessed value times the tax rate, and the Union County Board of Taxation certifies the rate. The collector cannot lower a tax or waive interest. Ask the Tax Office for the quarter-by-quarter status before closing so the title company can prorate correctly. The township's tax page links to a property tax relief page for owners who may qualify.

sections.h2: Getting around: roads, rail and Kean University
sections.html:
Union has about 145.85 miles of roads, crossed by the Garden State Parkway, Interstate 78, U.S. Route 22 and Route 82 on Morris Avenue. Parkway interchanges 139A, 139B, 140, 140A and 141 serve the township. The Union station on NJ Transit's Raritan Valley Line runs to Newark Penn Station, and its lot holds over 450 cars. Bus routes 113, 114 and 117 go to the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Midtown Manhattan, and Newark Liberty International Airport is about six miles east.

Kean University moved to the township in 1958 and serves almost 16,000 students, which keeps rental demand steady nearby. If your house is close to the station, a highway ramp or the campus, say so in the listing.

faqs.q: Is a resale certificate mandatory in Union, NJ?
faqs.a: Yes, the township requires a Residential Resale Certificate of continued occupancy before a sale. The inspection costs $175 and must be requested at least ten business days ahead.

faqs.q: How long does the Union resale certificate last?
faqs.a: It stays valid for three months from issue unless occupancy or ownership changes in the meantime. It cannot be transferred to another property or owner.

faqs.q: What does the Union inspector check?
faqs.a: The visit checks smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and fire extinguishers, and confirms that every open permit has been closed. Test the alarms before the inspector arrives.

faqs.q: What if my Union house fails the resale inspection?
faqs.a: A re-inspection costs $80, and the seller calls the housing inspector for a new appointment instead of reapplying. Fix the listed items first, since each extra visit adds cost and delay.

faqs.q: What are the Union tax due dates?
faqs.a: Bills fall due each February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, followed by a 10-day grace period, and postmarks earn no credit. Payments must be in the Tax Office by 4:30 p.m. to count that day.
